source.title: Generalizing Scaling Laws for Dense and Sparse Large Language Models
source.authors: Md Arafat Hossain; Xing-Fu Wu; Valerie E. Taylor; Ali Jannesari

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and symbols are imperfectly rendered in the extracted text, but the document is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper refits and compares scaling-law forms using datasets from prior work, arguing for a generalized dense-and-sparse law. Its comparisons also report differences between existing laws' predictions; it does not independently train new model sweeps.
record.gate_note: The reported comparisons and loss-trend descriptions use experimental datasets from [23]–[25], rather than newly trained runs. The ytopt-versus-grid-search discussion concerns coefficient-tuning results and does not provide extractable numerical outcomes. The DeepSeek-V3 IsoFLOP comparison uses interpolated predictions, not measured losses from an IsoFLOP training sweep.
record.test_reason: The study trains no models and never compares any law with measured losses. Every row compares one fitted formula's predictions with another's. The one result that bears on a version is that published dense and sparse laws give quite different losses at 0% sparsity, and that refitted exponents vary widely across datasets. This is weak T5 evidence for V7. V1 is not tested, because agreement between two formulas says nothing about whether observed loss follows a power law.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that their generalized law captures the behaviour of the dense (Hoffman), pruned (Frantar) and MoE (Abnar) laws, with small MSE between predictions. They say it can estimate the best N, D and C for a given sparsity, or the optimal sparsity for given N, D and C. They list the sparsity factor c and the coefficient γ as needing further optimization for larger models. The record should add that 'captures' means agreement with other laws' predictions, not with observed losses.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than independently reproducing the original training experiments, the paper refits and compares law forms using experimental datasets from prior work, including interpolated data for some comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted coefficients differ across the dense, pruned-model, and MoE datasets. The paper also compares coefficient tuning by ytopt with grid search and states that ytopt gives better loss predictions, but supplies no extractable numerical comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed sparsity-generalized law reproduces the predictions of the Frantar and Abnar laws closely (MSE 0.00078 and 0.0005), including predicted IsoFLOP sweet spots. It is never compared with measured losses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single sparsity-aware power-law form can emulate existing dense, pruned and MoE scaling-law formulas.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Symposium on Parallel & Distributed Processing, Workshops and Phd Forum
record.problems: The comparisons reuse results from earlier studies rather than reporting new training runs. Some Abnar data are interpolated from plots, and the DeepSeek-V3-scale comparison is predictive rather than empirically validated. No uncertainty estimates for the reported MSE values are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Figure 8's coefficient-tuning outcomes are discussed qualitatively but are not reported as numerical results in the text.

untested.parts: No observed held-out loss is fit or compared; only formula-to-formula agreement is reported.
No small-run fit is checked against larger observed runs. The DeepSeek-V3-scale curves are predictions only.
There is no estimate of how the optimal N and D scale with compute.
Sparsity laws are extended, but no other modality or regime is tested against data.
The study does not test whether curves bend away from a power law, and does not systematically test schedule or parameter-counting effects on the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Fitted coefficients of the proposed law differ greatly across the three datasets: α 0.34/0.28/0.08, β 0.28/0.08/0.40, e 1.69/0.15/0.57. This shows that exponents depend on data and setup.
missing.locator: Section IV-A, Tables VII, VIII, IX

missing.what: Coefficient fitting by ytopt is reported to give better loss fits than grid search, for Eqs. 2, 3 and 5. This is a fitting-method dependence, stated qualitatively with no numbers.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 'supports' label is dropped. All V1 evidence is law-versus-law, and r1 is identical to the Hoffman law by construction. The coefficient tables report 'fitted' values, but the text never says what they were fitted to, and no observed losses appear anywhere. Some Abnar inputs were interpolated from figures. Hoffman is misspelled in the paper (it should be Hoffmann), and Hoffmann et al. is an original source, but this study is not.

versions.untested_parts: Only scaling behavior represented by fitted laws on reused datasets is assessed; there is no independent training sweep across parameters, tokens, and compute.
No held-out small-run fit is evaluated against observed losses from runs orders of magnitude larger.
The paper compares IsoFLOP curves at particular compute budgets but does not establish how loss-minimizing parameter and token counts each scale as a stable power of compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No original experiments on other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The comparisons show prediction differences between selected laws and discuss coefficient fitting, but do not systematically test how exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary across fitting choices, schedules, and datasets, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: Hoffman et al. [23] dense-model dataset (9 models)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the proposed scaling law with the Hoffman law on the dense-model dataset
rows.measure: Calculated loss versus compute; comparison of the proposed law with the Hoffman law
rows.value: The plots are described as identical; both show decreasing loss as compute increases.
rows.note: The paper states the proposed law reduces exactly to the Hoffman law at 0% sparsity. The plotted dataset is reused from [23].
rows.check: This compares the proposed law with the Hoffman law, and by the paper's own Lemma the two are the same equation at S=0. The 'identical plot' is therefore circular. Loss is computed from the formula, not measured, so the row cannot bear on V1.

rows.subject: Frantar et al. [24] sparse-model dataset (48 models)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the proposed law's predictions with the Frantar scaling law on its experimental dataset
rows.measure: Loss prediction comparison and scaling trend
rows.value: The paper describes the scaling behavior as almost similar as sparsity and nonzero parameter count increase; average MSE = 0.00078.
rows.note: The underlying experiments are from [24]; the paper compares fitted-law predictions on that dataset.
rows.check: MSE=0.00078 is between two formulas' predictions, not between a formula and observed losses. This is the study's own method compared with another law, not a test of power-law loss.

rows.subject: Abnar et al. [25] MoE-model dataset (35 models)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the proposed law's predictions with the Abnar scaling law on an interpolated dataset
rows.measure: Loss prediction comparison and scaling trend
rows.value: The paper reports that loss decreases as sparsity and compute increase, with a similar pattern from both laws; average prediction MSE = 0.0005.
rows.note: The paper says it generated an interpolated dataset from plots in [25] because model-size and token lists were not shared.
rows.check: MSE=0.0005 is between two formulas' predictions, on inputs interpolated from plots in [25]. It is a law-to-law agreement value, not observed loss.

rows.subject: Frantar scaling-law predictions compared with Hoffman scaling-law predictions
rows.operation_detail: Compare the two laws at zero sparsity
rows.measure: Mean squared error between predicted losses
rows.value: Frantar scaling-law predictions differ; average MSE = 3.04.
rows.note: The comparison concerns predictions from the two fitted laws, not a new training run.
rows.check: Subject is the Frantar law (Eq. 4, refit) against the Hoffman law at 0% sparsity. The MSE of 3.04 is between two published laws' predictions, not measured losses. It is valid only as evidence that published laws disagree. The laws were fit on different data (C4/T5-style versus MassiveText), which likely explains much of the gap; the paper does not discuss this.

rows.subject: Abnar scaling-law predictions compared with Hoffman scaling-law predictions
rows.operation_detail: Compare the two laws at zero sparsity

conditions.value: Abnar et al. [25] model-size and data-size settings

rows.measure: Mean squared error between predicted losses
rows.note: The paper describes the Abnar dataset as using interpolated values for this comparison.
rows.check: Same caveat as r4: the MSE of 1.06 is between the Abnar and Hoffman law predictions at 0% sparsity, on the Abnar settings. It is not compared with observed loss.

rows.subject: Abnar et al. [25] MoE IsoFLOP models
rows.size_stated: Active parameters plotted up to 4B; the paper says the original experiments included approximately 26B active parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Compare IsoFLOP loss predictions across active parameter counts at fixed sparsity
rows.measure: Training loss versus active parameter count
rows.value: At fixed sparsity, loss decreases as active parameters increase until a sweet spot, then increases; the proposed law is described as capturing this behavior.
rows.note: This fixed-budget, fixed-sparsity IsoFLOP shape does not measure the stable power-of-compute allocation trend specified in V3.
rows.check: The IsoFLOP curves are formula predictions at one budget, not measured losses. They cannot show how the optimal N and D scale with compute (V3).

rows.subject: DeepSeek-V3-based interpolated IsoFLOP setting
rows.operation_detail: Generate and compare IsoFLOP predictions using the proposed and Abnar laws
rows.value: The proposed law is described as exhibiting a very similar pattern to the Abnar law.
rows.note: This is an interpolated prediction comparison, not observed loss from a larger training run.
rows.check: These are purely predicted IsoFLOP curves on an interpolated grid. 'Partial' is not a meaningful state here, and there is no observed loss.

relationships.condition: Published sparse laws (Frantar, Abnar) evaluated at 0% sparsity, compared with the Hoffman law
relationships.reason: Published laws built on the same Hoffman base give clearly different dense-limit losses: MSE 3.04 for Frantar (r4) and 1.06 for Abnar (r5). Refitted exponents also vary widely across datasets (from the text, Tables VII–IX). This is weak evidence: it is computed from published formulas, not new runs.
relationships.display_finding: At zero sparsity, Frantar and Abnar formulas differ from the Hoffman law with MSE of 3.04 and 1.06, respectively, and refitted exponents vary widely across datasets; the dense-limit comparison is calculated from published formulas rather than new training runs.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The paper reports decreasing-loss trends with increasing compute in the dense case and similar fitted-law scaling behavior in the sparse datasets (r1–r3).
